summary: Priscila Andre de Oliveira, a senior software engineer at Sentry based in Vienna, presents her daily AI workflow in Sentry's complex codebase, founded in 2010 with 15+ years of code, ~400 employees, and 100,000 dependent organizations. Since December 2025 she has shifted to only prompting, not hand-coding. Sentry has gone all-in on AI internally, producing tools like Abacus (AI usage tracking), Warden (code review agent), and Junior (a Slack bot that analyzes threads and creates fix PRs). The company also ran a three-month quality quarter to reduce technical debt, removing `any` types, to-dos, and unused feature flags. With ~100 PRs merged daily, the codebase is a moving target requiring constant re-alignment of understanding. She analyzed 116 of her own Claude sessions and found 67% were comprehension and only 2% were code generation, surprising even herself. Because her comprehension prompts kept repeating, she built a local skill called 'catch me up,' structured as a detailed markdown prompt with six exploration modes: architecture, conventions, feature traces, syntax, testing, and history. She demos it on an unfamiliar AI SDK testing repository, asking it to explain how the repository works and clarify what it simulates versus intercepts. Drawing on Jack Nation's blog post about 'vibe coding' and Rich Hickey's 'simple made easy,' she argues that the standard research-planning-implementation pipeline is missing a critical step: the engineer must understand what the agent found during research before letting it plan and implement. She cites Armin Ronacher's concern about people not knowing what code is in their own codebase. Her key takeaway: align your mental model before you prompt, use AI as the cheapest senior engineer who never tires of questions, and ship 'keynote code' rather than 'slop code' into the codebase that pays your salary.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Priscila introduces herself as a Brazilian senior software engineer at Sentry based in Vienna, a Verdaccio maintainer, and Vienna JS co-organizer. She jokes about promoting herself to 'agent manager' since she now only prompts, not codes. She shows recent contributions made with Claude including features, refactors, and cross-repository work.

sections.title: Sentry's engineering environment and scale
sections.summary: Sentry has grown from error and performance monitoring into a full observability platform with metrics, profiling, and agentic monitoring. Founded in 2010, it has 15+ years of code, ~400 employees, and 100,000 dependent organizations. She emphasizes she depends on the codebase for her salary and refuses to ship slop code.

sections.title: AI-driven projects at Sentry
sections.summary: During a hackathon, Sentry built several AI tools: Abacus (internal AI usage tracking), Warden (code review agent in PRs), Junior (Slack bot that analyzes bug reports and creates fix PRs), and an AI SDK testing repository where she was instructed to only prompt, not hand-code.

sections.title: Maintaining code quality and technical debt
sections.summary: Sentry ran a three-month quality quarter to remove TypeScript any types, to-dos, unused feature flags, and simplify code. With ~100 PRs merged daily and ongoing component deprecation, the codebase is a moving target requiring constant re-alignment of understanding.

sections.title: The role of comprehension in software development
sections.summary: She explains that ~70% of development involves understanding. AI made her faster by replacing manual git blame and Slack questions with instant prompt-based answers for incident tracking and product decisions. She notes the importance of steering AI when it misunderstands the codebase.

sections.title: Analyzing AI usage patterns
sections.summary: She had Claude analyze her cache of 116 sessions, classifying them into six categories. The result: 67% comprehension, only 2% code generation. This surprised her and motivated her to formalize her comprehension prompts.

sections.title: The 'Catch Me Up' skill architecture
sections.summary: She created a local skill called 'catch me up' as a detailed markdown prompt with six exploration modes: architecture, conventions, feature trace, syntax, testing, and history. It outputs structured tables and organograms to help her visually understand codebase structure.

sections.title: Short demo of the 'Catch Me Up' skill
sections.summary: She demos the skill on an unfamiliar AI SDK testing repository, prompting it to catch her up on how the repository works and clarify whether it simulates or intercepts Sentry envelopes. The skill returns a summary, flow diagram, and specific answers. She uses it also for PR review context.

sections.title: Planning vs. implementation in AI workflows
sections.summary: Referencing Jack Nation's blog post on vibe coding and Rich Hickey's 'simple made easy,' she argues the standard research-planning-implementation pipeline is missing a step: the engineer must understand what the agent found before letting it plan and implement.

sections.title: Conclusion and key takeaways
sections.summary: She cites Armin Ronacher's concern about people not knowing their own codebase. Her core message: the biggest AI unlock is comprehension, not generation. She urges tracking your own AI usage, using AI as the cheapest senior engineer, aligning your mental model before prompting, and shipping keynote code rather than slop code.
